current: "Thulium is rarer in the crust than silver or iodine."
corrected: "Thulium is rare, yet it is more common in the crust than silver or iodine."
source: CRC Handbook crustal abundances (via Wikipedia 'Abundance of elements in Earth's crust'): Tm 0.52 mg/kg, Ag 0.075 mg/kg, I 0.45 mg/kg; also the entry's own crustAbundancePpm 0.52
reason: The statement is backwards. At 0.52 ppm, thulium is about 7 times more abundant than silver (0.075 ppm) and slightly more abundant than iodine (0.45 ppm). It also contradicts the entry's own crustAbundancePpm.

source: Wikipedia 'Isotopes of samarium' (NUBASE-based table and footnote): Sm-149 is observationally stable, with expected alpha decay to Nd-145 at a half-life over 2×10^15 years
reason: The established experimental lower limit for Sm-149 is >2×10^15 y, not >10^16 y. The current value overstates the limit fivefold. The corrected wording matches the dataset's style for W-180m.

source: Wikipedia 'Isotopes of europium'; Belli et al. 2007 (Nucl. Phys. A 789, 15) and Casali et al. 2014 ('Discovery of the 151Eu alpha decay'): Eu-151 alpha-decays with half-life about 4.6×10^18 y
reason: Eu-151 has been observed to decay, so the stated convention puts it under radioactive. That is how the dataset treats W-180 (1.8×10^18 y), Bi-209, Nd-150 and Mo-100. Eu-153 stays stable, and displayA 153 is still fine.

corrected: [{"A":151,"halfLife":"4.6×10^18 years","note":"47.81% of natural europium; its very slow alpha decay was first seen in 2007."},{"A":152,"halfLife":"13.5 years","note":""}]
source: Wikipedia 'Isotopes of europium' (Eu-151 half-life 4.6×10^18 y, alpha decay found in 2007); IUPAC isotopic abundance 47.81%
reason: This goes with moving Eu-151 out of the stable list. A long-lived, naturally occurring radioactive isotope belongs under radioactive, with its abundance given in the note.

source: Wikipedia Promethium infobox (dhcp, hP4; older value a = 365 pm, c = 1165 pm; current infobox a = 363.93 pm, c = 1173.9 pm); WebElements
reason: The real structure is double hexagonal close-packed (the entry's own bulk.structure says so), and its c is about 1165 pm. The value 582.5 is half of that, the c of the simplified hcp drawing model. The convention says cPm is c of the real structure. Note that La, Pr and Nd in elements-06.json use the same halved c, so this may be a systematic pipeline choice; if it is fixed, fix all four.

source: Wikipedia 'Isotopes of holmium' (NUBASE2020): Ho-166m1 half-life 1132.6(39) y
reason: 1,200 y is an older evaluation, and the current evaluated value is 1,133 y, about 6% lower. That is outside the 2% tolerance, though some older handbooks still print 1,200 y.

current: Thulium is rarer in the crust than silver or iodine.
corrected: "Although it is a rare lanthanide, thulium is more common in the crust than silver or iodine."
source: CRC Handbook crustal abundances: Tm 0.52 mg/kg, I 0.45 mg/kg, Ag 0.075 mg/kg (this entry's own crustAbundancePpm is 0.52)
reason: The statement has it backwards. Thulium (about 0.5 ppm) is more abundant in Earth's crust than iodine (0.45 ppm) and roughly seven times more abundant than silver (0.075 ppm).

source: CRC Handbook / WebElements: Pm dhcp a = 365 pm, c = 1165 pm; Wikipedia infobox gives a = 363.9 pm, c = 1173.9 pm
reason: The structure is correctly given as double hexagonal close-packed, but 582.5 pm is half of the real dhcp c axis, which is about 1165 pm. It looks like the c value of the simplified hcp drawing model was entered. The convention says cPm must be c of the real structure.

current: Nuclear batteries for pacemakers and space probes (historically)
source: Wikipedia 'Betacel' and 'Promethium'; Physics Today, 'Betavoltaic power sources'
reason: Pm-147 Betacel batteries did power more than 100 pacemakers in the 1970s. Space-probe power is only described as a possible use, and Pu-238 became the standard there. No record shows Pm batteries actually flew on space probes, so 'historically' is misleading for that part.

current: Without erbium amplifiers, transoceanic fiber-optic internet would need far more repeater stations.
corrected: "Erbium amplifiers boost light directly, so one undersea fiber can carry many signal colors without converting them to electricity."
source: TAT-8 (1988) used electronic regenerators about every 40 to 70 km (around 100 over 6,657 km); EDFA undersea systems (TAT-12/13 onward) used similar or shorter amplifier spacings
reason: Erbium amplifiers did not greatly cut the number of repeaters. Older optoelectronic regenerators were spaced about as far apart. What EDFAs changed was all-optical amplification of many WDM wavelength channels at once, at any bit rate, so the claim about 'far more repeater stations' is misleading.

current: Terbium compounds glow bright green and its alloy Terfenol-D changes shape in a magnetic field more than any other material.
corrected: "Terbium compounds glow bright green and its alloy Terfenol-D changes shape in a magnetic field more than any other material at room temperature."
source: Wikipedia 'Magnetostriction' (Terfenol-D has the highest known magnetostriction of any alloy, about 2,000 microstrain at room temperature); patent literature reports Tb0.6Dy0.4 at about 6,300 ppm, but only at cryogenic temperatures
reason: Terfenol-D holds the record only at room temperature. Some Tb-Dy alloys and single crystals show larger magnetostriction at low temperatures, so the unqualified 'any other material' is false.

current: Detected spectroscopically; isolated by Lecoq de Boisbaudran in 1886.
corrected: "Detected spectroscopically; Lecoq de Boisbaudran isolated its oxide in 1886."
source: Wikipedia 'Gadolinium' (history): Lecoq de Boisbaudran separated gadolinia (the oxide) in 1886; Félix Trombe first isolated the metal in 1935
reason: In 1886 only the oxide (gadolinia) was obtained, and the metal was not isolated until 1935. Saying the element was 'isolated' in 1886 misleads students.

source: Johnson 2019 origin-of-elements chart; s-process (AGB) solar fractions from Arlandini et al. 1999 / Bisterzo et al. 2014: Er about 16-17% s-process, Gd about 15%
reason: Erbium's slow-neutron-capture share (about 16-17%) is at least as large as gadolinium's (about 15%), and this file lists 'dying low-mass stars' for Gd. Johnson's chart shows a low-mass-star share for Er. The list is inconsistent and incomplete, and the originNote 'made mostly by rapid neutron capture' already implies a second source.

source: Johnson 2019 origin-of-elements chart; Arlandini et al. 1999 s-process fractions (Dy about 15% s-process, about the same as Gd)
reason: Dysprosium's s-process (AGB-star) share is about the same as gadolinium's, and Gd is listed with 'dying low-mass stars'. Leaving it off Dy is inconsistent with the chart and with Dy's own originNote ('mostly' rapid neutron capture).
